target: AG1’s claim that school dissection usually uses already-dead animals and meat-industry byproducts rather than animals caught in the wild.
objection: AG2 says dissection supply typically depends on live wild capture followed by killing, so the practice is not just about already-dead byproducts.

target: AG2’s claim that school dissection practices typically depend on live wild capture and thus cause biodiversity harm.
objection: AG1 argues that standard school specimens are usually already-dead byproducts, so school dissection does not typically depend on live wild capture or cause the biodiversity harm AG2 describes.

target: AG1’s assumption that biodiversity harm does not follow if specimens are already dead by the time students dissect them.
objection: AG2 replies that if the animals were wild-caught, biodiversity harm occurred when they were removed from ecosystems, and that harm is not erased by the fact that the specimens are dead when dissected.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection’s environmental cost is biodiversity loss from wild capture rather than useful waste diversion.
objection: AG1 argues that when dissection uses meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills, the practice mainly diverts waste and does not require live wild capture, so biodiversity-loss reasoning does not apply to typical classroom dissection.

target: AG1’s waste-diversion framing of typical dissection specimens as environmentally beneficial byproducts.
objection: AG2 counters that even byproduct specimens come from meat production, which itself causes biodiversity loss and ecosystem damage, so landfill diversion does not remove the upstream environmental harm.

target: AG2’s claim that biodiversity loss from meat production is an impact attributable to classroom dissection.
objection: AG1 responds that using existing byproducts does not increase livestock production or meat demand for the school, so any biodiversity harm belongs to the meat-industry baseline rather than to classroom dissection itself.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection mainly involves waste diversion rather than biodiversity harm because the specimens are byproducts.
objection: AG2 argues that using meat-industry byproducts still supports the meat-production supply chain and therefore still makes the biodiversity harm part of dissection’s environmental impact.

target: AG2’s claim that biodiversity harm from meat production is the relevant environmental cost of dissection.
objection: AG1 says typical classroom dissection mainly changes the fate of already-dead byproducts, and since it does not initiate new animal production, the upstream meat-production biodiversity harm should not be treated as the dissection’s own key environmental cost.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection is mainly productive waste diversion rather than biodiversity harm.
objection: AG2 argues that buying and using meat byproducts still supports the meat-production supply chain that causes biodiversity loss, so the environmental impact cannot be reduced to waste diversion alone.

target: AG2’s claim that biodiversity harms from the broader meat supply chain matter more than waste diversion in classroom dissection decisions.
objection: AG1 maintains that in typical classroom cases the dissection activity mostly diverts already-dead byproducts from landfills and does not itself add incremental biodiversity harm, so biodiversity harm is not the decisive factor for the classroom decision.

target: AG1’s general defense of dissection as educationally worthwhile despite environmental framing.
objection: AG2 argues that dissection is not necessary for required curriculum or medical training, that alternatives teach biology as well or better, and that the harms outweigh any educational rationale.

target: AG2’s claim that comparable learning makes dissection unnecessary.
objection: AG1 says alternatives may cover some biology content, but they do not replicate the tactile manipulation, fine motor practice, and hand-eye coordination that real dissection provides.

target: AG1’s claim that dissection’s educational value justifies it despite alternatives.
objection: AG2 responds that those practical skills can be taught with non-animal lab models, and that because harmless alternatives can teach the same goals, dissection is not educationally necessary.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection’s educational case is defeated by the availability of alternatives.
objection: AG1 says real dissection also motivates students and can spark science career interest through “aha moments,” so comparable content learning alone does not eliminate the educational case for dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that classroom dissection is educationally justified and should therefore be required.
objection: AG2 argues that requiring students to dissect real animals necessarily supports inhumane animal-supply methods, and if equally effective alternatives exist, the requirement is unjustified.

target: AG2’s claim that typical school dissection necessarily supports inhumane animal treatment.
objection: AG1 says standard classroom specimens are usually already-dead byproducts, so dissection does not necessarily involve live-animal killing or the inhumane sourcing AG2 assumes.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is unjustified because it necessarily involves inhumane sourcing.
objection: AG1 argues that in typical classroom cases the ethical concern is largely mitigated because specimens come from already-deceased or byproduct sources, and dissection still offers distinct educational and motivational benefits.

target: AG1’s claim that using already-dead or byproduct specimens removes the ethical problem.
objection: AG2 says that even if the specimens are already dead, requiring students to use them still participates in the inhumane animal-supply chain that produced them.

target: AG1’s claim that typical dissection specimens are not primarily wild-caught and therefore do not cause biodiversity loss.
objection: AG2 argues that the supply chain usually begins with wild capture and that the fact students receive already-dead specimens does not erase the biodiversity harm from how those animals were obtained.

target: AG2’s claim that the biodiversity-loss argument applies to typical classroom dissection.
objection: AG1 responds that typical specimens are mostly already-dead meat-industry byproducts, not wild-caught animals removed from ecosystems, so the specific biodiversity-loss mechanism does not apply to normal classroom dissection.

target: AG1’s claim that already-dead/byproduct specimens avoid inhumane and environmentally harmful sourcing.
objection: AG2 says that even already-dead byproduct specimens still require participation in the inhumane and environmentally harmful supply chain that produced them.

target: AG2’s claim that the educational benefits of dissection can be fully matched by alternatives.
objection: AG1 argues that synthetic models and simulations cannot fully replicate the tactile tissue manipulation, practical skill-building, and real-world dissection experience that real animal dissection provides.

target: AG1’s claim that extra educational benefits justify dissection even when standards do not require it.
objection: AG2 replies that the curriculum standards and medical-training systems cited do not require animal dissection, so any extra benefits do not make it necessary for required learning outcomes.

target: AG2’s claim that dissection is an avoidable inhumane practice.
objection: AG1 says that in typical school settings dissection uses already-dead byproducts rather than animals killed specifically for the classroom, so it is not a classroom live-killing practice.

target: AG1’s claim that using byproduct specimens avoids the harms of dissection.
objection: AG2 argues that byproduct specimens still come from slaughtered animals and therefore still involve students in the inhumane meat-supply chain that produced them.

target: AG2’s claim that students’ participation in dissection is still inhumane even with byproduct specimens.
objection: AG1 says that when specimens are already-dead byproducts, dissection does not add new inhumane treatment beyond the meat-industry baseline, and it still provides educational value.

target: AG1’s claim that already-dead/byproduct dissection is ethically acceptable and educationally worthwhile.
objection: AG2 says that even with byproduct specimens, required dissection remains inhumane and unnecessary because the learning goals can be met with non-animal alternatives.

target: AG2’s claim that alternatives make dissection unnecessary and ethically unjustified.
objection: AG1 argues that real dissection gives distinctive tactile and practical learning benefits that models and simulations cannot fully replicate, making dissection educationally worthwhile.

target: AG1’s claim that typical dissection specimens are not wild-caught and therefore avoid biodiversity harm.
objection: AG2 says that even if the specimens arrive already dead, their origin typically involves wild capture, so the biodiversity harm still exists and dissection should not be required when alternatives are available.
